answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 (1975) and its reglamento DS 597 (1984), as they stood in the 1996-10-22 and 1998-05-18 versions, give detained or expellable foreigners no right to communicate with their consul. The only consular mention in the expulsion chapter is DL 1.094 art. 85: the consular representative may arrange the exit of deserting crew members. The VCCR, promulgated by Decreto RR.EE. 709 of 28 Nov 1967, was in force but was not counted by the 2020 coder. There is no practice evidence for this period.

Same texts. The 2002-05-31 amendment of DL 1.094 (Ley 19.806, art. 35) touched only art. 94, on courts and Gendarmeria reporting rulings on foreigners, not consular contact. There is no practice evidence.
No change. The DS 597 version of 2000-05-23 and the DL 1.094 version of 2002-05-31 were in force; neither contains a consular-communication rule. There is no practice evidence.

Ley 20.430 (2010) and Ley 20.507 (2011) amended DL 1.094 (refugee provisions; art. 33 bis residence for trafficking victims) but added no consular-access rule. The CMW 2011 Concluding Observations mention consuls only in recommending that Chilean consular officials be informed of migrants' Convention rights. The consular rule the 2023 coding relies on (Ley 21.325 art. 134) only came into force in February 2022.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: Searched the DL 1.094 versions (1996-10-22, 2002-05-31, 2010-04-15, 2011-04-08) and the DS 597 versions (2000-05-23 and the last version) for 'consular' and 'consul'. The only consular references concern visas, the Arancel Consular, official residents and crew members (DL art. 85). DS 518/1998 (penitentiary regulation) has no consular provision either. No consular-communication protection existed and was repealed between 2000 and 2020.

answers.starting_answer_concern: Chile promulgated the VCCR by Decreto RR.EE. 709 of 28 November 1967 (cited in the recitals of the Reglamento Consular, Decreto 172/1977), and promulgated treaties apply in Chile's legal order. The MRD's own Argentina and Colombia examples code 'Yes' on VCCR ratification alone. On that basis Chile's 2020 answer (and the answers back to 2000) could arguably have been 'Yes'. The 2020 'No' against the 2023 'Yes' reflects the coder's reliance on Ley 21.325 art. 134 (in force February 2022), not a change in the treaty position.
answers.notes: The answer rests on statutes and regulations only; no ruling was relied on. The VCCR was not counted, consistent with the 2020 starting answer (see concern). There is no practice evidence specific to consular access in 2000-2015.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 arts. 81-90 and DS 597 arts. 167-176 allow control measures and detention of 'el afectado' / 'el extranjero' pending expulsion, with no exception for minors. Neither text contains 'menores de edad' in this context. There is no practice evidence on child detention for this period.
Unchanged. The 2002 amendment of DL 1.094 (art. 94) does not concern minors or detention. There is no practice evidence.
Unchanged. Ley 20.430 (published and in force 15-04-2010) postdates this date. There is no practice evidence.

Ley 20.430 (2010) gives asylum-seeking children family-unity and non-sanction protections but no prohibition on detaining migrant children; DL 1.094 and DS 597 are unchanged on detention. The CMW 2011 Concluding Observations raise detention generally (lack of data on length and conditions) without a finding on children.

answers.repealed_search: Searched DL 1.094 (versions 1996-2011) and DS 597 (versions 2000-05-23 and last) for 'menor de edad' and 'menores de edad' and for any exception to detention or expulsion for children; none found. Ley 20.430 mentions minors only in family unity. No protection existed and was repealed between 2000 and 2020.

practice_sources.title: CMW Concluding observations on the initial report of Chile (CMW/C/CHL/CO/1)

answers.sourcing_note: DL 1.094 and DS 597 were read from LeyChile JSON with version metadata; the DS 597 art. 174/176 text in the 2000-05-23 version is identical to the last version. Ley 20.430 was read only in its current text. There is no practice evidence on detention of migrant children for 2000-2015.
answers.notes: The answer rests on statutes and regulations; no ruling relied on. The CRC (promulgated 1990) was not counted, consistent with the starting answer.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 81 subjects foreigners who entered irregularly or overstayed to 'control inmediato', and art. 84 provides for their transfer. Art. 89 (text from Ley 18.252, 1983) says that while an expulsion appeal is pending 'el extranjero afectado permanecerá privado de su libertad en un establecimiento carcelario'. DS 597 arts. 174 and 176 add 'restricciones y privaciones de su libertad que sean estrictamente necesarias'. There is no practice evidence for this period.
Unchanged. The only DL 1.094 amendment in 2000-2005 (Ley 19.806, 2002) concerned art. 94. There is no practice evidence.
Unchanged detention provisions. There is no practice evidence for this date.

Detention provisions unchanged by Ley 20.430 (2010) or Ley 20.507 (2011). Practice confirms detention: the CMW in 2011 noted migrants held in 'administrative custody' with no information on length or conditions. In March 2013 the Corte Suprema upheld an amparo freeing 17 migrants held over 15 days at the PDI Borgoño station pending expulsion (press report).

answers.repealed_search: Searched the DL 1.094 versions (1996-10-22, 2002-05-31, 2010-04-15, 2011-04-08; arts. 81-90 carry only Ley 18.252/1983 annotations) and the DS 597 versions (2000-05-23, 2015-03-07, last; arts. 174/176 unchanged) for any prohibition or limit on immigration detention. None found; both texts expressly authorise detention pending expulsion. Ley 20.430's non-sanction rule covers refugees only and is not a ban on detention.
